text: Let's begin our Lesson 3, and how to break down your goal.

In this lecture, we will learn why goals alone fail, the three-level system (3-month, monthly, and weekly), what the system gives us, and two examples of how to break down your goal, and at the end, some practical rules.
Having a goal is such a crucial part for us to go forward, but just having a goal alone doesn't mean that you will be able to complete
the goal itself.
You will not be able to really succeed only if you have a goal, and there's a couple of reasons why just the goal alone may fail.
The first one is because the goal is too vague to guide your daily action—it's too big to guide your daily action, you don't even know where to start, and the goal has no clear next steps.
What happens is that there comes a decision fatigue: you don't know what to do, you don't know where to start, and then there is no
and then, when there is no timeline, urgency disappears.
You don't really have something to push you because you have this amount of time left to complete this, and then there's no tracking.
And when there is no tracking, effort feels pointless, and then trying to change everything at once becomes a burnout.

You know, trying to complete your goal, your big goal, whatever it is, immediately becomes a burnout because it's too big—you don't know where to start, you don't know how to track it, you don't know what is your next step, and the
one which comes from that, or after that, is that there is no progress.
And then, when there is no progress, there's overwhelm, and then there's avoidance, and then again, you abandon the goal.
As we said in the previous lecture, we just start something and you just lay it off—you just completely start a new thing, or you just find out that you don't want to do this.
And one of the reasons is because the goal is not really broken down, and so for that, we will be using the three levels to structure any goal.
We will be using the
3-month goal, so this is the first layer, and this is the main outcome that you want in the next 3 months.
And the second layer, or the second level, is the monthly goal—the chunk you will do this month to move forward to the 3-month goal.
So these are the goals, or these are the tasks, which you will do in these three months to move you forward to the 3-month goal, to the big goal which you have.
And then we have the third layer, or the third level, which is weekly goals:
What's a small, finishable thing you will do this week to move you forward to this month's goal?
So again, all of these three are connected together, and this creates a clear path.
You know where you're going in the next 3 months, where to focus on this month, and exactly what to do this week.
And also, daily planning will become a part of this system, but just later, after some lectures.
And what this system gives us is that it gives us
direction for the next 3 months, and it gives us, again, a monthly rhythm and a weekly execution.
It gives us less overwhelm because our focus is so much more narrow, our focus is so much sharper, and we can see exactly what we need to do.
And in general, it will give us so much more motivation; it will give us so much more control.
And the reason why it will give us motivation is because we will complete something much faster,
and we will see that we are doing something weekly or monthly, and then that will motivate us so much more.
It will drive us so much more to go and finish this whole 3-month goal which we have.
And a thing to note is that the month and the week—the plan of the month and the week—are changeable.
And the reason it changes is because the main focus is just going to be to complete the 3-month goal.
So whatever you need to
change to, let's say, achieve that 3-month goal, you can go and do it.
You can change your weekly plan; you can change your monthly plan or goals if you know that this will move you forward, or faster, or better, to achieve the 3-month goal which you have.
